In college, I had a field trip to the Cliff Walk in Newport. The geology professor told us this amazing fact, which I just checked with these Google search terms: were the rocks in Newport RI once part of Africa according to geologists?
AI Overview begins: Yes, according to geologists, the bedrock under Newport, Rhode Island was once part of an ancient landmass connected to Africa.
All of Rhode Island—including the famous coastal rock formations along Newport’s Cliff Walk—sits atop an exotic chunk of continental crust known as Avalonia (or the Avalon Terrane).

The Journey from Africa to New England

• The African Origin: Roughly 600 million years ago, the rocks that now make up Newport were part of a volcanic island chain forming along the coast of Gondwana, an ancient supercontinent that included modern-day Africa and South America.
• The Breakup and Drift: Sometime between 500 and 700 million years ago, this ribbon of land broke away from Gondwana and drifted across a long-vanished ocean.
• The Collision: Around 400 million years ago, Avalonia collided with and welded itself onto the eastern margin of Laurentia (ancient North America). When the continents later collided again to create the supercontinent Pangaea, these rocks were crushed and folded.
• The Split: When Pangaea eventually broke apart about 200 million years ago to create the modern Atlantic Ocean, the rift didn't form exactly where the old boundaries were. Instead, it left pieces of Avalonia stranded on both sides of the ocean. While most of Gondwana snapped back to become Africa, Newport and the rest of eastern New England remained firmly attached to North America.
